newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices edge up but outlook still neutral.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices edge up but outlook still neutral.

text.p: World oil prices edged a few cents higher on Wednesday but the outlook for the next few weeks remains broadly neutral, oil dealers said.
London June futures for bellwether North Sea Brent crude settled nine cents up at $18.16 a barrel at 1915 GMT.
"The market has sat in range for six weeks now. So its hard to get worked up one way or the other," said Nigel Saperia, managing director of the oil division at Bankers Trust International.
Brent futures have stayed in a narrow $1.21 a barrel range either side of $18 since the beginning of April.
Dealers say the market is balanced between faltering demand for diesel in Asia and expectations of a seasonal pick up in gasoline demand in the United States.
Those expectations were given a boost by the latest inventory figures for gasoline from the United States.
On Wednesday the Energy Information Agency (EIA) reported a stock draw of 2.4 million barrels, confirming a 3.6 million barrel draw reported on Tuesday by the American Petroleum Institute.
Gasoline demand in the United States is expected to rise to a record 8.14 million barrels per day (bpd) this summer, up 1.8 percent from last summer, the EIA reported last month.
But many dealers remained relaxed despite the possibility of gasoline demand in the U.S. tugging world crude oil prices higher.
Western refineries are returning to full production after heavy repair work and are enjoying ample crude supply with prompt cargoes selling at discounted prices.
This should ensure even the most rampant U.S. gasoline demand is met, particularly from Europe which produces 10 percent more than it needs.
But while refiners are enjoying a wide diet of crude oil, Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries ministers are wrestling with the problems of overproduction.
OPEC's ministerial output monitoring committee met on Wednesday to discuss the 11-member group's quota compliance.

Ministers declined comment ahead of the meeting which will examine media estimates showing runaway OPEC production of nearly 27 million bpd, or nearly two million bpd above the groups self imposed ceiling of 25.033 million bpd.

The former OPEC Secretary-General Subroto of Indonesia said on Wednesday the group should formally dump its outdated policy of setting strict oil output quotas and make revenue its sole policy objective.
"OPEC should state its clear cut objective is to optimise revenue," he said while attending an oil and gas conference in Iran.
"I would suggest that OPEC could work more smartly to optimise revenues. In other words, not a strict quota policy."

For many OPEC members OPEC quotas already appear a thing of the past. Countries like Venezuela and Qatar have preferred to boost capacity by courting foreign investment and maximising market share while ignoring the consequences for oil prices.

Many OPEC watchers wonder whether the cartel will ever set a realistic ceiling again. Only Saudi Arabia and, to a lesser extent, its Gulf allies Kuwait and United Arab Emirates maintain any significant spare capacity.
"Oil markets (are) expected to be in fragile equilibrium during May," said oil consultants The Petroleum Finance Company (PFC).
But "this will be gradually undermined by rising stocks and higher crude oil output by the end of the second quarter," said PFC in its latest Global Oil Markets report.

The International Energy Agency (IEA), the West's oil "watchdog", expects oil production from countries outside the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) to rise by 0.7 million bpd in the third quarter this year.
But despite overproduction by OPEC, demand in the third quarter is expected to rise by 0.9 million bpd after falling by 2.4 million in the second, the IEA said in it's most recent report.
